quotes.t: Thou hast made me endless, such is thy pleasure. This frail vessel thou emptiest again and again, and fillest it ever with fresh life.
The grass seeks her crowd in the earth. The tree seeks his solitude of the sky.
It is the tears of the earth that keep her smiles in bloom.
Poverty is the parent of revolution and crime.
No one would choose to live without friends, even if he had all other goods.
Virtue is a state of character concerned with choice, lying in a mean.
Empty your cup so that it may be filled; become devoid to gain totality.
A teacher is never a giver of truth; he is a guide, a pointer to the truth that each student must find for himself.
Running water never grows stale. So you just have to keep on flowing.
You act like mortals in all that you fear, and like immortals in all that you desire.
Wealth is the slave of a wise man, the master of a fool.
A gift consists not in what is done or given, but in the intention of the giver or doer.
The reports of my death are greatly exaggerated.
quotes.source: Cable to the New York Journal, 1897

quotes.t: If you pick up a starving dog and make him prosperous he will not bite you. This is the principal difference between a dog and man.
Man is the only animal that blushes. Or needs to.
If you want to be successful, find someone who has achieved the results you want and copy what they do and you'll achieve the same results.
The meeting of preparation with opportunity generates the offspring we call luck.
I believe life is constantly testing us for our level of commitment, and life's greatest rewards are reserved for those who demonstrate a never-ending commitment to act until they achieve.
The pendulum of the mind oscillates between sense and nonsense, not between right and wrong.
The word happy would lose its meaning if it were not balanced by sadness.
We meet ourselves time and again in a thousand disguises on the path of life.
The need for change bulldozed a road down the center of my mind.
quotes.source: I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings

quotes.t: Words mean more than what is set down on paper. It takes the human voice to infuse them with deeper meaning.
quotes.source: I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings

quotes.t: The caged bird sings of freedom.
A coward is incapable of exhibiting love; it is the prerogative of the brave.
Man becomes great exactly in the degree in which he works for the welfare of his fellow men.
To believe in something, and not to live it, is dishonest.
I never travel without my diary. One should always have something sensational to read in the train.
To lose one parent may be regarded as a misfortune; to lose both looks like carelessness.
The only excuse for making a useless thing is that one admires it intensely.
If you have an important point to make, don't try to be subtle or clever. Use a pile driver. Hit the point once. Then come back and hit it again. Then hit it a third time, a tremendous whack.
The inherent vice of capitalism is the unequal sharing of blessings; the inherent virtue of socialism is the equal sharing of miseries.
I am easily satisfied with the very best.
Never let yourself be saddened by a separation.
Be indifferent to where you live.
Never stray from the Way.
Self-pity is our worst enemy and if we yield to it, we can never do anything wise in this world.
The highest result of education is tolerance.
Life is a succession of lessons which must be lived to be understood.
The opportunity to defeat the enemy is provided by the enemy himself.
Thus the expert in battle moves the enemy, and is not moved by him.
In war, the way is to avoid what is strong and to strike at what is weak.
Talk to yourself once in a day, otherwise you may miss meeting an intelligent person in this world.
All love is expansion, all selfishness is contraction. Love is therefore the only law of life.
Truth can be stated in a thousand different ways, yet each one can be true.
The best brains of the nation may be found on the last benches of the classroom.
Science is a beautiful gift to humanity; we should not distort it.
Learning gives creativity, creativity leads to thinking, thinking provides knowledge, and knowledge makes you great.
Luck is a matter of preparation meeting opportunity.
Passion is energy. Feel the power that comes from focusing on what excites you.
I trust that everything happens for a reason, even when we're not wise enough to see it.
Understanding is a two-way street.
Life was meant to be lived, and curiosity must be kept alive. One must never, for whatever reason, turn his back on life.
What you don't do can be a destructive force.
Nature never breaks her own laws.
Study without desire spoils the memory, and it retains nothing that it takes in.
He who wishes to be rich in a day will be hanged in a year.
Two nations; between whom there is no intercourse and no sympathy.
What is earnest is not always true; on the contrary, error is often more earnest than truth.
Everything comes if a man will only wait.
If all men knew what others say of them, there would not be four friends in the world.
I paint objects as I think them, not as I see them.
In every real man a child is hidden that wants to play.
We must use time wisely and forever realize that the time is always ripe to do right.
Love begins by taking care of the closest ones, the ones at home.
The soul has illusions as the bird has wings: it is supported by them.
The purpose of a writer is to keep civilization from destroying itself.
Living is easy with eyes closed, misunderstanding all you see.
A pessimist is a man who thinks everybody is as nasty as himself, and hates them for it.
One must learn by doing the thing, for though you think you know it, you have no certainty until you try.
Man is a clever animal who behaves like an imbecile.
Ability is nothing without opportunity.
We think that the point is to pass the test or to overcome the problem, but the truth is that things don't really get solved. They come together and they fall apart.
Do not be concerned with the faults of other persons.
The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation.
Citizenship consists in the service of the country.
Music is a moral law. It gives soul to the universe, wings to the mind, flight to the imagination, and charm and gaiety to life and to everything.
I was really too honest a man to be a politician and live.
We must cultivate our garden.
Suffering has been stronger than all other teaching, and has taught me to understand what your heart used to be. I have been bent and broken, but — I hope — into a better shape.
Because I could not stop for Death, he kindly stopped for me.
Lost time is never found again.
I have a dream that my four little children will one day live in a nation where they will not be judged by the color of their skin but by the content of their character.
I must learn to be content with being happier than I deserve.
The strongest of all warriors are these two: Time and Patience.
That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.
We must guard against the acquisition of unwarranted influence, whether sought or unsought, by the military-industrial complex.
If men were angels, no government would be necessary.
Remember the ladies, and be more generous and favourable to them than your ancestors.
The life of man is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.
The greatest happiness of the greatest number is the foundation of morals and legislation.
quotes.source: An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation

quotes.t: I am all in a sea of wonders. I doubt; I fear; I think strange things, which I dare not confess to my own soul.
Beautiful, beautiful. Magnificent desolation.
One must be absolutely modern.
In every human breast, God has implanted a principle, which we call love of freedom.
Women belong in all places where decisions are being made.
Look for the helpers. You will always find people who are helping.
We are what we pretend to be, so we must be careful about what we pretend to be.
Real courage is when you know you're licked before you begin, but you begin anyway and see it through no matter what.
Once a king or queen of Narnia, always a king or queen of Narnia.
quotes.source: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe

A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.bio: Indian aerospace scientist and the 11th President of India (2002-2007), known as the 'Missile Man of India'.

Abigail Adams.bio: American writer, wife of President John Adams and mother of President John Quincy Adams, known for her advocacy for women's rights.

Albert Camus.bio: French-Algerian writer and philosopher, author of The Stranger; Nobel Prize in Literature 1957.

Albert Schweitzer.bio: Albert Schweitzer was an Alsatian theologian, musician and physician who founded a hospital at Lambaréné in Gabon and served there for decades. His philosophy of reverence for life and his Bach scholarship earned him the Nobel Peace Prize in 1952.

Aristotle.bio: Greek philosopher and student of Plato; founder of logic and many scientific fields.

Arthur Rimbaud.bio: French poet, author of A Season in Hell and Illuminations.

Benjamin Disraeli.bio: British statesman who served twice as Prime Minister and led the Conservative Party. He was also a successful novelist, writing books such as Coningsby and Sybil.
Benjamin Disraeli.credit: Cornelius Jabez Hughes, Public domain (File: File:Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield.jpg)

Benjamin Franklin.bio: American polymath - printer, scientist, diplomat - and a Founding Father of the United States.

Blaise Pascal.bio: French mathematician, physicist and philosopher, author of the Pensées.
Blaise Pascal.credit: unknown; a copy of the painting of François II Quesnel, which was made for Gérard Edelinck en 1691, Public domain

Bram Stoker.bio: Irish author, best known for the novel Dracula (1897).

Bruce Lee.bio: Bruce Lee was a Hong Kong-American martial artist and actor who transformed martial-arts cinema with films such as Enter the Dragon. His philosophy of adaptability — 'be water' — blended Taoist ideas with his own Jeet Kune Do.
Bruce Lee.credit: National General Pictures, Public domain (File: File:Bruce Lee 1971 National General Pictures publicity photo.jpg)

Buzz Aldrin.bio: American astronaut and lunar module pilot of Apollo 11, the second person to walk on the Moon in 1969.

C. S. Lewis.bio: C. S. Lewis was an Irish-born scholar and writer at Oxford, author of The Chronicles of Narnia, Mere Christianity and The Screwtape Letters. A close friend of Tolkien, he moved from atheism to Christianity and became one of its most popular modern interpreters.

Carl Jung.bio: Swiss psychiatrist who founded analytical psychology. His concepts of the collective unconscious, archetypes and introversion and extraversion remain influential in psychology and culture.
Carl Jung.credit: AnonymousUnknown author, Public domain (File: File:CARL JUNG (1875 - 1961).jpg)

Charles Dickens.bio: English novelist and social critic; author of A Christmas Carol, Oliver Twist and Great Expectations.

Dogen.bio: Founder of the Sōtō school of Zen in Japan and author of the Shōbōgenzō, a landmark of Buddhist philosophy.

Dwight D. Eisenhower.role: General and President of the United States
Dwight D. Eisenhower.bio: American general and the 34th President of the United States (1953-1961).

Eleanor Roosevelt.bio: Eleanor Roosevelt was the longest-serving First Lady of the United States, from 1933 to 1945, and reinvented the role as a platform for civil rights and social reform. Afterward she became a US delegate to the United Nations and chaired the commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
Eleanor Roosevelt.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author, Public domain (File: Eleanor Roosevelt portrait 1933.jpg)

Emily Dickinson.bio: American poet whose nearly 1,800 poems, mostly unpublished in her lifetime, made her a central figure of American literature.
Emily Dickinson.credit: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress, Public domain

Fred Rogers.bio: American television host (1928–2003) of the children's program Mister Rogers' Neighborhood.

Friedrich Nietzsche.bio: German philosopher known for Thus Spoke Zarathustra and the concept of the will to power.

George Bernard Shaw.bio: Irish playwright and critic; author of Pygmalion; Nobel Prize in Literature 1925.
George Bernard Shaw.credit: Sussman, Public domain (File: George Bernard Shaw, playwright (SAYRE 9001).jpg)

Harper Lee.bio: Harper Lee (1926–2016) was an American novelist whose 1960 novel To Kill a Mockingbird won the Pulitzer Prize and became one of the best-selling books of all time.

Helen Keller.bio: American author and activist who, deaf and blind from childhood, became a renowned advocate for disability rights.
Helen Keller.credit: Los Angeles Times; restored by User:Rhododendrites, Public domain

Henry David Thoreau.bio: American writer known for Walden (1854) and the essay Civil Disobedience.

James Madison.role: Statesman and President of the United States
James Madison.bio: American statesman, the 4th President of the United States, and a principal author of the Constitution.

Jane Austen.bio: English novelist known for Pride and Prejudice and Emma, celebrated for irony and social observation.
Jane Austen.credit: Engraving by William Home Lizars after James Andrews, Public domain

Jawaharlal Nehru.bio: Leader of India's independence movement and the country's first Prime Minister (1947-1964).

Jeremy Bentham.bio: English philosopher and founder of utilitarianism.

John Lennon.bio: English singer-songwriter, co-founder of the Beatles and solo artist known for Imagine.

Kurt Vonnegut.bio: Kurt Vonnegut (1922–2007) was an American novelist and satirist whose darkly comic books, including Slaughterhouse-Five and Cat's Cradle, blended science fiction with anti-war themes.

Leo Tolstoy.bio: Russian novelist, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

Leonardo da Vinci.bio: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian Renaissance painter, engineer and anatomist whose notebooks reveal an insatiable curiosity about nature and art. He painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, and filled thousands of pages with studies, inventions and observations.
Leonardo da Vinci.credit: Leonardo da Vinci, Public domain (File: Leonardo self.jpg)

Mahatma Gandhi.bio: Leader of India's nonviolent independence movement; pioneered satyagraha and became the father of the Indian nation.

Mark Twain.bio: American writer (Samuel Clemens) known for Adventures of Huckleberry Finn and The Adventures of Tom Sawyer.

Martin Luther King Jr..bio: American Baptist minister who led the civil rights movement; Nobel Peace Prize laureate 1964.

Maya Angelou.bio: American poet and memoirist best known for I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings (1969).
Maya Angelou.credit: Bee Photos by Ryan Marty, Public domain

Miyamoto Musashi.bio: Legendary Japanese swordsman, undefeated in over sixty duels, author of The Book of Five Rings and the Dokkodo.

Mother Teresa.bio: Albanian-Indian Catholic nun who founded the Missionaries of Charity in Kolkata; Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1979).
Mother Teresa.credit: John Mathew Smith & www.celebrity-photos.com from Laurel  Maryland, USA, CC BY-SA 2.0

Napoleon Bonaparte.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution and became Emperor of the French in 1804. His Napoleonic Wars reshaped Europe, and his Napoleonic Code influenced legal systems worldwide. He died in exile on Saint Helena.

Neil Armstrong.bio: American astronaut and the first person to walk on the Moon, during Apollo 11 in 1969.

Nelson Mandela.role: Anti-apartheid leader, President of South Africa
Nelson Mandela.bio: South African anti-apartheid revolutionary who spent 27 years in prison and became the country's first Black president in 1994.

Oprah Winfrey.bio: American talk-show host and media executive whose long-running show made her one of the most influential broadcasters in history.
Oprah Winfrey.credit: US Embassy South Africa, Public domain

Oscar Wilde.bio: Irish playwright, poet and author of The Picture of Dorian Gray, famed for his wit and epigrams.
Oscar Wilde.credit: Napoleon Sarony (restoration by Adam Cuerden), Public domain

Pablo Picasso.bio: Pablo Picasso was a Spanish artist who co-founded Cubism and reinvented his style across a career of nearly eighty years. Works such as Les Demoiselles d'Avignon and Guernica made him the most famous and influential artist of the 20th century.
Pablo Picasso.credit: Didier Descouens, Public domain (File: File:(Barcelona) Retrat de Picasso - Pablo Gargallo - Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya.jpg)

Pema Chodron.bio: Pema Chodron is an American nun in the Tibetan Buddhist tradition and a widely read author and teacher. Her books, including When Things Fall Apart, bring Buddhist teachings on compassion and difficulty to a broad audience.

Phillis Wheatley.bio: American poet, the first published African-American woman poet, author of Poems on Various Subjects (1773).

Plato.bio: Greek philosopher, student of Socrates and author of The Republic.

Rabindranath Tagore.bio: Bengali poet and polymath from India; the first non-European Nobel laureate in Literature (1913), known for Gitanjali.

Ruth Bader Ginsburg.bio: American jurist (1933–2020), associate justice of the U.S. Supreme Court.

Seneca.bio: Roman Stoic philosopher and statesman, author of Letters to Lucilius.

Socrates.bio: Greek philosopher of Athens, central figure of Western philosophy; left no writings.

Sophocles.bio: Sophocles was an Athenian tragedian who wrote more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete. Oedipus Rex and Antigone, his most famous works, set the pattern for Western tragedy.

Sun Tzu.bio: Ancient Chinese general traditionally credited with The Art of War, a treatise on strategy studied worldwide for over two thousand years.
Sun Tzu.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (File: 吴司马孙武.jpg)

Swami Vivekananda.bio: Indian Hindu monk who introduced Vedanta and Yoga to the West; famous for his 1893 Chicago Parliament of Religions address.
Swami Vivekananda.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (File: Swami Vivekananda at Parliament of Religions.jpg)

Tony Robbins.bio: Tony Robbins is an American author, coach and motivational speaker known for bestselling books such as Unlimited Power and Awaken the Giant Within. His seminars and self-help programmes have made him one of the most prominent figures in the personal development industry.

Victor Hugo.bio: French poet and novelist, author of Les Misérables and The Hunchback of Notre-Dame.
Victor Hugo.credit: Étienne Carjat, Public domain (File: Victor Hugo by Étienne Carjat 1876 - full.jpg)

Voltaire.bio: Voltaire, born François-Marie Arouet, was a French Enlightenment writer, philosopher and historian famous for the novella Candide and for his witty defence of civil liberties, including freedom of speech and religion. He was one of the most prolific and influential writers of his age.

Winston Churchill.bio: British prime minister during the Second World War and Nobel laureate in Literature.
